sobolev-acl-characterization — ACL characterization of first-order Sobolev functions [theorem]
  For an open Ω⊂ℝⁿ and1≤p≤∞, f∈W¹,ᵖ(Ω) exactly when f∈Lᵖ has a representative absolutely continuous on compact subintervals of almost every coordinate-parallel line in Ω, with its almost-everywhere classical partial derivatives in Lᵖ. Those derivatives are its weak partial derivatives.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- First-order Sobolev space W¹,ᵖ [statement]: Absolute continuity is local along almost every coordinate slice; the global Lp conditions are stated separately.
  <- Absolutely continuous function on a real interval [statement]: Absolute continuity is local along almost every coordinate slice; the global Lp conditions are stated separately.
  <- Fubini’s theorem for integrable functions [proof]: On each rectangle compactly contained inΩ, use product test functions and Fubini in the weak derivative identity. A countable dense collection of one-dimensional tests gives, on almost every coordinate line, the one-dimensional weak identity. Subtract the indefinite integral of that slice’s L¹ derivative: its distributional derivative is zero, hence it is constant and the slice has an absolutely continuous representative. A countable rectangular cover gives the local slice assertion. Conversely, integrate by parts on the absolutely continuous slices and then apply Fubini; the Lp partials are weak derivatives. For continuous homeomorphisms, equality almost everywhere on each good slice identifies this representative with the given restriction.
  <- Fundamental theorem of Lebesgue integration [proof]: On each rectangle compactly contained inΩ, use product test functions and Fubini in the weak derivative identity. A countable dense collection of one-dimensional tests gives, on almost every coordinate line, the one-dimensional weak identity. Subtract the indefinite integral of that slice’s L¹ derivative: its distributional derivative is zero, hence it is constant and the slice has an absolutely continuous representative. A countable rectangular cover gives the local slice assertion. Conversely, integrate by parts on the absolutely continuous slices and then apply Fubini; the Lp partials are weak derivatives. For continuous homeomorphisms, equality almost everywhere on each good slice identifies this representative with the given restriction.
  <- Distributions with zero derivative on an interval [proof]: On each rectangle compactly contained inΩ, use product test functions and Fubini in the weak derivative identity. A countable dense collection of one-dimensional tests gives, on almost every coordinate line, the one-dimensional weak identity. Subtract the indefinite integral of that slice’s L¹ derivative: its distributional derivative is zero, hence it is constant and the slice has an absolutely continuous representative. A countable rectangular cover gives the local slice assertion. Conversely, integrate by parts on the absolutely continuous slices and then apply Fubini; the Lp partials are weak derivatives. For continuous homeomorphisms, equality almost everywhere on each good slice identifies this representative with the given restriction.
  explains in hencl-pratelli-2015, §4 grid-side selection and(4.46); complete weak-slicing proof supplied in008-proof-notes.txt — The specified proof is examined here; this is not a claim that the theorem originated in this source.
  relies_on in hencl-pratelli-2015, §4.2 and(4.46) — The weak Sobolev derivative is used as the derivative of restrictions to almost all selected line segments.

anova-product-decomposition — ANOVA decomposition on a product probability space [definition]
  For square-integrable f(X₁,…,X_n) with independent inputs, define f_∅=Ef and f_u=E[f|X_u]−∑_{v⊊u}f_v. Then f=∑_uf_u; nonconstant components have zero conditional mean after integrating any one of their active coordinates, and distinct components are orthogonal in L².

abel-summation — Abel's summation formula [theorem]
  If Aₖ=∑ⱼ₌₁ᵏaⱼ, then ∑ₖ₌₁ᴺaₖbₖ=A_N b_N+∑ₖ₌₁ᴺ⁻¹Aₖ(bₖ−bₖ₊₁).
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: formalized; estimated LOC: 86.0
    Evidence: Mathlib 26573066084e6e2aa8526ea358bc43b66d96f970. Finset.sum_range_by_parts':71–84 in Algebra/BigOperators/Module proves sum_i f_i*g_i=(sum_i f_i)*g_(N-1)-sum_(i<N-1)(sum_(j<=i)f_j)*(g_(i+1)-g_i). Actual complete induction proof read. Set f_i=a_(i+1),g_i=b_(i+1),N>=1, and rewrite minus a difference as b_k-b_(k+1): this is exactly A_N*b_N+sum_(k=1..N-1) A_k*(b_k-b_(k+1)). No smooth interpolation or integral summation formula is required. N=0 is the empty-sum convention with A0=0, not an invalid last-term use. Relevant actual declarations, hypotheses and indicated completed proof bodies inspected; bounded existing-source review without new proof development or rebuild.
Search and boundary notes: Compared finite index shift and endpoint convention explicitly. NumberTheory/AbelSummation is the related continuous-integral version, not necessary to prove the finite identity.

Native TauCeti.sum_Icc_rpow_mul_eq284–317 proves the direct ordinary power-weight Abel form with floor-indexed partial sums and real upper endpoint. Complete proof handles x<1 by empty sums and otherwise applies the actual derivative/integrability/Abel integral identity; this is associated summation-by-parts API, not a claim that an arbitrary arithmetic application was formalized. Relevant actual declarations, hypotheses and indicated completed proof bodies inspected; bounded existing-source review without new proof development or rebuild.
Search and boundary notes: Enumerated native NumberTheory/AbelSummation and ArithmeticDirichletSeries/AbelSummation siblings. Select direct generic power-weight formula; L-series asymptotics/summability applications are separate endpoints and excluded.

algebraic-group-action-variety — Action of an algebraic group on an algebraic variety [definition]
  An action of an algebraic group G on an algebraic variety X over k is a morphism μ:G×_k X→X with μ∘(e×id_X)=id_X and μ∘(m×id_X)=μ∘(id_G×μ) as morphisms G×G×X→X; on R-points it gives actions of the groups G(R) on X(R). For a k-point x the orbit map G→X is g↦μ(g,x), and the orbit of x is its image in X.

  <- Group action on a set [statement]: The two commuting diagrams are the identity and compatibility axioms of a group action, holding on R-points for every k-algebra R.
  <- Rational point of a scheme [statement]: Orbit maps are attached to k-points x∈X(k), and the action is described on R-points.

addition-theorem-spherical-harmonics — Addition theorem for spherical harmonics [theorem]
  For n≥3 and an orthonormal basis Y₁,…,Y_N of degree-k real spherical harmonics under probability-normalized area, ∑ⱼYⱼ(u)Yⱼ(v)=N G_{k,n}(u·v), where G_{k,n} is the normalized zonal Gegenbauer polynomial with G_{k,n}(1)=1. adelic-mahler-compactness-criterion — Adelic Mahler compactness criterion [theorem]
  A fixed-covolume family of F-lattices in an adelic finite-dimensional vector space is relatively compact modulo F-linear changes of basis exactly when the family has a common positive lower bound on lengths of nonzero rational lattice vectors.

  <- Compactness of adelic quotients of unipotent groups [proof]: Triangular matrices with diagonal in a compact set are compact modulo rational triangular matrices: the unipotent part uses compactness of N(A)/N(ℚ).

affine-coxeter-complex-root-system — Affine Coxeter complex of a crystallographic root system [construction]
  For an irreducible reduced finite crystallographic root system Φ, the affine Coxeter complex is the Euclidean simplicial tessellation cut out by hyperplanes ⟨x,α⟩=k for α∈Φ,k∈ℤ. Its maximal cells are alcoves, and its walls are the reflecting hyperplanes. The affine Weyl group acts simply transitively on alcoves; labeling one alcove’s vertices by opposite walls and propagating by this action gives its vertex types.

affine-weyl-group-alcove-coxeter-complex — Affine Weyl groups as Coxeter groups on alcoves [theorem]
  For an irreducible reduced finite crystallographic root system, the affine Weyl group W_a, with the set S of reflections in the walls of a fixed alcove, is a Coxeter system acting simply transitively on alcoves, and the affine Coxeter complex is W_a-equivariantly isomorphic to the Coxeter complex Σ(W_a,S). In particular every proper standard parabolic subgroup ⟨T⟩, T⊊S, is finite.

affine-building — Affine building [definition]
  An affine building is a typed simplicial complex equipped with apartments isomorphic to one affine Coxeter complex, such that any two simplices lie in an apartment and any two apartments have a type-preserving simplicial isomorphism fixing their intersection pointwise. Apartment intersections are convex in their Euclidean realizations. It is thick if each codimension-one chamber face lies in at least three chambers, and locally finite if each vertex belongs to finitely many simplices.

  <- Convergence to equilibrium for finite irreducible aperiodic Markov chains [proof]: Write p_n for the law at n, c_n=min_xp_n(x)/π(x), and c_{−1}=0. Stationarity gives c_n≥c_{n−1}. Conditional on not having stopped before n, the unnormalized state mass is p_n−c_{n−1}π. Stop in statex with probability (c_n−c_{n−1})π(x)/(p_n(x)−c_{n−1}π(x)), using independent uniforms; interpret0/0 as0. The stopped mass at(n,x) is exactly(c_n−c_{n−1})π(x). Hence X_T is stationary and independent ofT, whileP(T>n)=1−c_n=sep(p_n,π); convergence to equilibrium ensuresT<∞ a.s. Conversely any strong stationary time has p_n(x)≥P(T≤n)π(x), giving its required tail lower bound.

aleph-cardinals — Aleph sequence of infinite cardinals [definition]
  The alephs enumerate infinite well-ordered cardinalities: ℵ₀ is countable infinity, ℵ_{α+1} is the least larger infinite cardinal, and at a limit ordinal λ, ℵ_λ=sup_{α<λ}ℵ_α.

  <- Spectral theorem for a real symmetric matrix [proof]: Lemma 4.1 is reduced to diagonal Z by an orthogonal change of basis, and the self-adjoint matrix A on ℓ²(p) is analysed through its eigenvectors and eigenvalues.
  <- Perron–Frobenius theorem for nonnegative matrices [proof]: A has positive entries (Lemma 2.6(e)) and A1=1, so by Perron–Frobenius 1 is its largest eigenvalue with unique eigenvector 1.
  <- Reverse Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for a form of positive index at most one [proof]: Lemma 2.8 (hyperbolic quadratic forms, 2⇒1) turns Lemma 4.1 for the quadratic form (Z,Z′)↦D(Z,Z′,I,M₂,…) into the reverse Cauchy–Schwarz inequality claimed.

nilsequence-algebra-closure — Algebra and uniform closure of nilsequences [theorem]
  For a fixed d≥1, basic d-step nilsequences form a complex algebra stable under conjugation and integer shifts; the same is true with no step bound. Their uniform closures, the d-step nilsequences and nilsequences, are uniformly closed algebras with the same invariances.

algebraic-variety-field — Algebraic variety over a field [definition]
  An algebraic variety over a field k is a scheme X with a separated morphism of finite type X→Spec k that is geometrically reduced: its base change to an algebraic closure of k is reduced, i.e. its rings of sections have no nonzero nilpotent elements. Varieties need not be irreducible, connected or affine. Over an algebraically closed field this means a reduced separated k-scheme of finite type.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Morphism of schemes of finite type [statement]: A variety is an algebraic scheme, i.e. of finite type over Spec k.
  <- Separated morphism of schemes [statement]: Varieties are required to be separated over k.
  <- Base change and fibers of a scheme [statement]: Geometric reducedness is reducedness of the base change X×_k k̄ to an algebraic closure (algebraic closure inherited through scheme-base-change).
  <- Reduced commutative ring [statement]: Reducedness of a scheme means its rings of sections, equivalently its local rings, are reduced rings.
  explains in milne-algebraic-groups-2017, Appendix A.44 — Selected learning reference; not a priority claim.
  Related: Affine algebraic variety over a field — The catalogue’s affine variety (reduced finitely generated coordinate algebra) is the affine case of an algebraic variety, up to the geometric-reducedness convention.

reductivity-closed-orbit-base-extension — Algebraically closed base-extension invariance of reductivity and closed orbits [theorem]
  For affine algebraic data over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field, extending to a larger algebraically closed field preserves and reflects reductivity of a smooth affine group and geometric closedness of an orbit of an algebraic action.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: False
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Characteristic of a field [statement]: Characteristic zero is assumed.
  <- Reductive affine algebraic group, allowing components [statement]: The property preserved and reflected is reductivity.
  <- Orbit and stabilizer of an algebraic group action [statement]: Geometric closedness of an orbit is the second property compared.

algebraically-independent-subset — Algebraically independent subset of a field extension [definition]
  A subset S of a field extension L/K is algebraically independent over K if no nonzero polynomial with coefficients in K vanishes when evaluated at finitely many distinct elements of S; otherwise S is algebraically dependent over K.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Field extension [statement]: Algebraic independence is relative to a field extension L/K.
  <- Polynomial ring over a commutative ring [statement]: Independence means no nonzero polynomial over K in several variables vanishes on elements of S.
  <- Subset [statement]: The notion applies to subsets of L.

almost-holomorphic-modular-form — Almost holomorphic modular form [definition]
  For a specified congruence subgroup and integer weight k, a function obeying the scalar modular weight-k transformation, polynomial in 1/Im(τ) with holomorphic coefficients and of at most polynomial growth in Im(τ) after normalization at every cusp. This is the almost holomorphic convention called nearly holomorphic by Larson, and excludes cusp poles.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: formalized; estimated LOC: 662.2
    Evidence: Mathlib 26573066084e6e2aa8526ea358bc43b66d96f970. Exact generic primary predicate on f:SlashInvariantForm Γ k (SlashInvariantForms:36, which imposes NO holomorphy) is ∃N and holomorphic coefficient functions a_j:ℍ→ℂ, j:Fin(N+1), with ∀τ,fτ=∑j,a_jτ*((τ.im:ℂ)⁻¹)^(j.val); holomorphic means the actual MDifferentiable ℂ map predicate used by ordinary modular forms. The real Im τ is strictly positive on ℍ, so the finite polynomial in its inverse is literal. Require after EVERY cusp normalization γ (equivalently all SL2Z normalizations for the given congruence group), ∃Nγ:ℕ, (f|[k]γ)=O[comap UpperHalfPlane.im atTop](τ↦(τ.im)^Nγ). Actual SL_slash_apply:171 gives the precise scalar weight-k slash; IsBigO:86/IsBigOWith:72 is the exact eventual constant-times-power norm bound. This is the paragraph’s bare almost-holomorphic convention and excludes cusp poles through the explicit growth condition, without falsely requiring f itself holomorphic. The polynomial exponent j.val is a nonnegative integer; the inverse is taken BEFORE that natural power. This makes the coefficient-field and exponent convention explicit.

schwartz-dyadic-almost-orthogonality — Almost orthogonality of dyadically dilated Schwartz kernels [theorem]
  If φ,ψ∈S(ℝⁿ) both have vanishing moments below the integer L≥0 and φⱼ(x)=2ʲⁿφ(2ʲx), ψₖ(x)=2ᵏⁿψ(2ᵏx), then for every M>0, |φⱼ*ψₖ(x)|≤C2^{−L|j−k|}2^{n min(j,k)}(1+2^min(j,k)|x|)⁻ᴹ. For j≥k only φ needs the moment condition; for k≥j only ψ does. Constants may depend on the fixed kernels, L,M,n, but not j,k,x.

  For a real matrix A and real column b, exactly one holds: Ax=b for some column x with every coordinate strictly positive; or there is a real column p with Aᵀp≥0, pᵀb≤0, and at least one strict inequality among these scalar inequalities.

ample-invertible-sheaf — Ample invertible sheaf [definition]
  An invertible sheaf L on a scheme X of finite type over a field is ample if for every coherent sheaf F the sheaves F⊗L^(⊗n) are generated by global sections for all large n. For proper X this holds exactly when some tensor power L^(⊗n), n≥1, is very ample.

analytic-continuation-along-path — Analytic continuation along a path [definition]
  Given a path γ:[0,1]→ℂ, an analytic continuation along γ is a family of holomorphic functions f_t on open disks containing γ(t) such that f_t and f_s agree on the overlap of their disks whenever s is close to t; f_1 continues f_0 along γ.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete

analytic-hypersurface-complex-manifold — Analytic hypersurface in a complex manifold [definition]
  A closed subset V of a complex manifold M such that each point of V has a connected open coordinate neighbourhood U on which V∩U is the zero set of a single holomorphic function U→ℂ that is not identically zero. V is irreducible if it is not the union of two analytic hypersurfaces each properly contained in V. Its smooth points are those near which such a local equation can be chosen with nonzero differential.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete

  <- Connected topological space [statement]: The local equation is required not to vanish identically on a connected neighbourhood.
  <- Complex partial derivative [statement]: Smooth points are defined by a local equation with nonzero differential.

inverse-function-theorem-local-field — Analytic inverse function theorem over a local field [theorem]
  For an analytic map between finite-dimensional manifolds over R,C or a finite extension of Q_p, an invertible derivative at a point gives an analytic local inverse. A surjective derivative gives local analytic sections after choosing complementary coordinates.

  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True

  <- P-adic local field [statement]: The nonarchimedean ground fields allowed are the finite extensions of Q_p.
  <- Complex number [statement]: The complex ground field is one of the allowed local fields.
  <- Valuation ring of a discretely valued field [proof]: After rescaling, all coefficients lie in the valuation ring, so the formal inverse has integral coefficients and converges on the unit polydisc.
  <- Complex power series [proof]: Cauchy’s method of majorants compares with explicitly inverted real power series that converge near 0, covering the real and complex cases.

analytic-map-local-field-manifolds — Analytic map between analytic manifolds over a local field [definition]
  For analytic manifolds X,Y over a local field K, a map f:X→Y is analytic if it is continuous and its expressions in charts are given near every point by convergent K-power series. Its derivative T_xf at x is the K-linear map whose matrix in charts is the Jacobian of first-order coefficients; f is an analytic isomorphism if it is bijective with analytic inverse.

complex-abelian-variety-analytic-uniformization — Analytic uniformization of a complex abelian variety [theorem]
  For a complex abelian variety A of dimension g, the exponential map identifies A(C) analytically with its complex tangent space modulo a lattice of rank2g. A homomorphism is induced by its complex-linear tangent map carrying the source lattice into the target lattice; for an endomorphism, an invertible tangent map is equivalent to having finite kernel and being an isogeny.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Analytification of a smooth projective complex variety [both]: A(C) is regarded as a compact connected complex Lie group, the analytification of the smooth projective group variety A; algebraic homomorphisms induce holomorphic homomorphisms.
  <- Exponential map of a commutative complex Lie group [both]: The statement uses the exponential map of the commutative complex Lie group A(C); Proposition 2.1(a) is exactly this holomorphic homomorphism with identity differential, used in the proof for surjectivity and the lattice kernel.
  <- Complex torus [statement]: The conclusion identifies A(C) with the complex torus Tgt₀A(C)/Λ, Λ a full lattice of rank 2g.
  <- Isogeny of abelian varieties [statement]: The final clause characterizes isogenies (surjective homomorphisms with finite kernel) among endomorphisms; homomorphisms of abelian varieties are inherited.
  <- Differential of a Lie group homomorphism [both]: The tangent map of a homomorphism is its differential at 0; the proof uses φ(exp v)=exp(dφ(v)), so φ is induced by dφ and dφ carries ker exp_A into ker exp_B.
  <- Analytic inverse function theorem over a local field [proof]: Because d(exp)₀ is the identity, the holomorphic inverse function theorem makes exp a local isomorphism at 0, giving an open image and a neighbourhood meeting ker exp only in 0.
  <- Connected topological groups are generated by identity neighbourhoods [proof]: The image of exp is an open, hence closed, subgroup of the connected group A(C), so exp is surjective.
  <- Projectivity of abelian varieties [proof]: An abelian variety is projective, so the analytification theorem for smooth projective complex varieties applies to A.
  <- Smith diagonalization of an integer matrix [proof]: For an endomorphism with invertible tangent map α, α(Λ)⊆Λ has finite index |det α| by choosing adapted bases; the kernel α⁻¹(Λ)/Λ≅Λ/α(Λ) is finite. Conversely a non-invertible α has kernel containing the infinite image of ker α in V/Λ, and an injective α is surjective, so finite kernel ⇔ isogeny.
  <- Structure of discrete subgroups of a finite-dimensional real vector space [proof]: ker exp is a discrete subgroup of the 2g-dimensional real space, hence a lattice; compactness of V/ker exp≅A(C) forces it to be full.

andreief-rank-one-determinant-integral — Andréief–Cauchy–Binet determinant identity for rank-one integrals [theorem]
  For an integrable rank-one covariance matrixM=∫vvᵀdν(v) inℝ^m, detM=(1/m!)∫⋯∫det(v₁,…,v_m)²dν(v₁)⋯dν(v_m), whenν is finite with bounded support.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Determinant of a square matrix [statement]: Both sides are determinants: of the m×m matrix M and of the vectors v₁,…,v_m.
  <- Transpose of a matrix [statement]: The rank-one matrices are vvᵀ.
  <- Lebesgue integral [statement]: M=∫vvᵀdν is an entrywise integral, and the right side is an integral.
  <- Product measure [statement]: The right side integrates against the m-fold product measure ν⊗⋯⊗ν.
  <- Euclidean space ℝᵈ [statement]: ν lives on ℝ^m; bounded support is defined by the Euclidean distance.
  <- Borel σ-algebra of a topological space [statement]: ν is a Borel measure on ℝ^m.
  <- Transpose invariance of the determinant [proof]: The remaining determinant is transposed so that the j-th row depends only on v_j.
  <- Fubini’s theorem for integrable functions [proof]: Summation and integration are interchanged and the integrals are performed row by row over the product measure (integrability from bounded support).
  <- Linearity of the Lebesgue integral [proof]: Integrating each row separately uses linearity of the integral in the multilinear determinant expansion.

arzela-ascoli-finite-dimensional — Arzelà–Ascoli theorem for Euclidean-valued paths [theorem]
  A uniformly bounded equicontinuous family inC([0,T];ℝᵈ) is relatively compact in the uniform norm.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Equicontinuous family of functions [both]: The hypothesis is equicontinuity of the family; the proof first upgrades pointwise equicontinuity on the compact interval to uniform equicontinuity by a finite subcover.
  <- Relatively compact subset of a topological space [statement]: The conclusion is relative compactness (compact closure) of the family in the uniform-norm topology.
  <- Euclidean space ℝᵈ [statement]: The paths take values in ℝᵈ with its Euclidean norm; uniform boundedness is boundedness of sup_t|f(t)|.
  <- Completeness of continuous Banach-valued function spaces [both]: C([0,T];ℝᵈ) is the Banach space of continuous maps of the compact metric space [0,T] into ℝᵈ with the supremum (uniform) norm; the proof concludes from completeness of C(I,ℝⁿ) that the uniformly Cauchy diagonal subsequence converges.
  <- Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem in ℝᵈ [proof]: At each point t_j of a countable dense set the bounded sequence x_m(t_j) has a convergent subsequence (Bolzano–Weierstraß), giving the diagonal subsequence.
  <- Density of the rationals in the reals [proof]: The proof uses a dense subset {t_j} of the interval, e.g. the rationals in I.
  <- Countability of the rational numbers [proof]: The dense set of rational times is enumerated as a sequence t_1,t_2,…, so the diagonal argument is countable.
  <- Heine–Borel theorem in finite-dimensional normed spaces [proof]: Compactness of the closed bounded interval I lets finitely many balls B_δ(t_j) cover it, and gives the finite subcover in the equicontinuity-to-uniform-equicontinuity step.
  <- Sequential characterization of compact metric spaces [proof]: In the metric space C(X→Y) precompactness is equivalent to sequential precompactness, so it suffices that every sequence in the family has a uniformly convergent subsequence.

atomic-molecular-variable-triebel-type — Atomic and molecular characterization of cube-weighted variable Triebel–Lizorkin spaces [theorem]
  For admissible p,q,s,φ, put c̃₁⁻¹≤φ(x,r)/φ(x,2r). If nonnegative integers K>s⁺+max(0,log₂c̃₁) and L>n/min(1,p⁻,q⁻)−n−s⁻, then sufficiently rapidly decaying uniformly normalized (K,L)-molecules synthesize matching dyadic coefficient sequences boundedly into F^{s(·),φ}_{p(·),q(·)}, with convergence in S′. Conversely every element has a smooth atomic expansion with coefficient quasi-norm bounded by its function-space quasi-norm, with arbitrarily prescribed nonnegative orders K,L; scale0 atoms require no cancellation.

variable-lebesgue-extrapolation-a1 — A₁ extrapolation into variable-exponent Lebesgue spaces [theorem]

extreme-hb-backward-shift-defect — Backward-shift defect identity in an extreme de Branges–Rovnyak space [theorem]
  If b is an extreme point of the unit ball of H∞, thenH(b) is invariant underLf=(f−f(0))/z and ∥Lf∥²_{H(b)}=∥f∥²_{H(b)}−|f(0)|² for everyf∈H(b).

  <- Backward shift on Hardy H² [both]: The operator L in the statement is the H² backward shift restricted to H(b)⊂H²; the proof uses ‖Lf‖²₂=‖f‖²₂−|f(0)|² in H².

  <- Two-component boundary model of a de Branges–Rovnyak space [proof]: Scalar case of Theorem 2.2(i): f∈H(b) has a unique partner g in clos(ΔH²) with b̄f+Δg⊥H² and ‖f‖²_b=‖f‖²₂+‖g‖²₂.   <- Logarithmic boundary integrability of nonzero Hardy H² functions [proof]: If clos(ΔH²)=θH² then Δ=|h| for a nonzero h∈H², so log Δ is integrable; this excludes the simply invariant case for extreme b (§2.5.1 dichotomy).
  <- Extreme-point criterion for the closed unit ball of H∞ [proof]: §2.5.1 identifies the simply invariant defect space with non-extreme b; via the criterion, integrability of log(1−|b*|²) means b is non-extreme, so extreme b gives clos(ΔH²)=L²(E), invariant under multiplication by ζ̄.
  <- Fatou boundary-value theorem for Hardy H² [proof]: The model lives in L² of the circle: boundary functions of H² identify H² isometrically with the nonnegative-frequency subspace, give b* and Δ=(1−|b*|²)^{1/2}, and (Lf)*=ζ̄(f*−f(0)).

banach-alaoglu-theorem — Banach–Alaoglu theorem [theorem]
  The unit ball of the continuous dual of a normed space is compact for pointwise convergence on that space, the weak-* topology. If the normed space is separable, this compact topology on the dual ball is metrizable and every bounded sequence has a weak-* convergent subsequence.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Weak-star topology on a continuous dual [statement]: The compactness is for the weak-star topology σ(X*,X) of pointwise convergence on X; this also brings in the continuous dual and its norm, which defines the unit ball.
  <- Subspace topology [statement]: The dual unit ball carries the weak-star topology restricted to it.
  <- Compact topological space [statement]: The conclusion is compactness of the dual ball.
  <- Separable metric space [statement]: The second assertion assumes the normed space is separable for its norm metric.
  <- Metric induced by a norm [statement]: Separability of a normed space refers to the metric d(x,y)=‖x−y‖.
  <- Topology induced by a metric [statement]: Metrizability means the weak-star topology on the ball is the topology induced by some metric.
  <- Pointwise convergence of functions [statement]: A weak-star convergent subsequence converges pointwise on X as functions to the scalar field.
  <- Tychonoff’s theorem [proof]: Theorem 4.53: the product K=∏_(x∈X)‖x‖·B_K of closed discs is compact by Tychonoff’s theorem.
  <- Heine–Borel theorem in finite-dimensional normed spaces [proof]: Each factor ‖x‖·B_K, a closed disc in ℝ or ℂ≅ℝ², is compact.
  <- Closed subsets of compact spaces are compact [proof]: Theorem 4.53: the image R is closed in the compact product, “and consequently compact”.
  <- Continuous image of a compact space [proof]: B_(X*)=φ⁻¹(R) is compact as the image of the compact R under the continuous inverse; in Proposition 4.54 the identity (B_(X*),weak*)→(B_(X*),d) maps closed (compact) sets to compact sets.
  <- Continuity of a uniform limit [proof]: Proposition 4.54: y*↦d(x*,y*) is weak-star continuous as a uniform limit of weak-star continuous partial sums.
  <- Compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces are closed [proof]: Proposition 4.54: compact subsets of the metric space (B_(X*),d) are closed, so the identity is a closed map and hence a homeomorphism.
  <- Hausdorff topological space [proof]: Metric topologies are Hausdorff, which is the hypothesis needed to close compact sets in (B_(X*),d).
  <- Sequential characterization of compact metric spaces [proof]: The remark before Proposition 4.54: compactness and sequential compactness agree for metric spaces, so in the separable case every bounded sequence, rescaled into the compact metrizable ball, has a weak-star convergent subsequence.

Within each state, empirical distributions on each class have diameter below ε; the unconditioned measure is regular as well.

split-primes-determine-galois-extension — Bauer’s theorem on split primes and Galois extensions [theorem]
  Let L and M be finite extensions of a number field K inside a fixed algebraic closure, with M/K Galois. If, apart from finitely many exceptions (or a set of Dirichlet density zero), every prime of K having a degree-one prime factor in L splits completely in M, then M⊆L. In particular two finite Galois extensions of K with the same split primes up to such exceptions coincide.

benatar-goldbach-prime-difference-dichotomy — Benatar’s Goldbach–prime-difference dichotomy [theorem]
  Either successive Goldbach numbers have bounded gaps beyond some point, or the set D of infinitely recurring positive prime differences has full relative density among the even integers, with |((2N)∖D)∩[1,N]|≪N^κ for some κ<1. Differences in D need not be consecutive prime gaps.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
    Evidence: Mathlib 26573066084e6e2aa8526ea358bc43b66d96f970. The actual inspected Bertrand theorem Nat.exists_prime_lt_and_le_two_mul:225 provides a prime in (n,2n], with a completed binomial-bound/finite-prime-cover proof. Native Tau fixed-congruence prime counting gives PNT for one modulus, not the catalogue dichotomy. No checked theorem supplies either eventual bounded gaps between Goldbach numbers OR the full-even-relative-density/power-saving exceptional count for infinitely recurring positive prime differences. This is an off-diagonal bound; the diagonal terms are retained when computing a full second moment.

bessaga-pelczynski-selection-principle — Bessaga–Pełczyński selection principle [theorem]
  In a Banach space with a Schauder basis, every seminormalized weakly null sequence has a subsequence equivalent to a seminormalized block sequence; the block vectors can be chosen to approximate that subsequence with any prescribed summable positive error bounds.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Seminormalized sequence in a normed space [statement]: Seminormalization is essential for equivalence; the statement is not asserted for an arbitrary norm-null sequence.
  <- Weak convergence in a Banach space [both]: Seminormalization is essential for equivalence; the statement is not asserted for an arbitrary norm-null sequence.
  <- Block sequence relative to a Schauder basis [statement]: Seminormalization is essential for equivalence; the statement is not asserted for an arbitrary norm-null sequence.
  <- Equivalent basic sequences [statement]: Seminormalization is essential for equivalence; the statement is not asserted for an arbitrary norm-null sequence.
  <- Uniform boundedness of Schauder partial-sum projections [proof]: Inductively choose an indexn_k beyond the previous subsequence index so its projection onto the firstm_(k−1) coordinates has norm less than half the prescribed error: finitely many continuous coordinates tend to0 by weak nullity. Then choose an endpointm_k so the tail ofx_(n_k) beyondm_k has norm less than the other half. The intervening coordinate blocks approximatex_(n_k). Seminormalization keeps block norms bounded above and away from0; choose errors small enough that the basic block coordinate bounds make the perturbation sum<1. The small perturbation principle gives equivalence. This is a complete curator-written gliding-hump proof of the actual selection tool silently used by the source.
  <- Small perturbation principle for basic sequences [proof]: Inductively choose an indexn_k beyond the previous subsequence index so its projection onto the firstm_(k−1) coordinates has norm less than half the prescribed error: finitely many continuous coordinates tend to0 by weak nullity. Then choose an endpointm_k so the tail ofx_(n_k) beyondm_k has norm less than the other half. The intervening coordinate blocks approximatex_(n_k). Seminormalization keeps block norms bounded above and away from0; choose errors small enough that the basic block coordinate bounds make the perturbation sum<1. The small perturbation principle gives equivalence. This is a complete curator-written gliding-hump proof of the actual selection tool silently used by the source.

bethe-free-energy-limit-decorrelation — Bethe free-energy limit under local Gibbs decorrelation [theorem]
  For a locally convergent sequence of bounded-degree typed factor models with finite spins and positive weights from a fixed finite family, assume every fixed short-cycle-free event has nonvanishing probability in both ordinary and locally conditioned partition-function-biased models. Let p be a consistent limiting-tree marginal assignment. If average two-variable Gibbs marginals converge in total variation to the corresponding products from p, then limsup n⁻¹ElnZ≤B(p). If the same holds in the locally conditioned partition-function-biased model, the limit equals B(p). Non-reconstruction implies the required decorrelation; uniform tree boundary-influence decay yields equality in both models.

beurling-deny-criteria — Beurling–Deny criteria for positivity-preserving and sub-Markov semigroups [theorem]
  Let H≥0 be self-adjoint on real L²(X,m) with closed form Q. beurling-cyclic-outer-criterion-h2 — Beurling’s characterization of cyclic functions in Hardy H² [theorem]
  A nonzero f∈H² of the unit disk has polynomial multiples dense in H² exactly when log|f*| is integrable on the circle and f(z)=c·exp∫(ζ+z)/(ζ−z)·log|f*(ζ)|dm(ζ) with |c|=1, where m is normalized arc measure. Thus the cyclic and the exponential definitions of outer functions agree in H².

bezuglyi-handelman-good-trace-density-criterion — Bezuglyi–Handelman density criterion for good traces [theorem]
  Let G be an approximately divisible dimension group with order unit and τ a trace. Then τ is good with respect to order units if and only if the image of ker τ under the affine representation is norm dense in {τ}^⊢, the continuous affine functions on the normalized trace space vanishing at τ. For simple G every nonzero positive element is an order unit, so this characterizes good traces.

bezuglyi-handelman-refinability-goodness-relations — Bezuglyi–Handelman relations between refinability, goodness and kernel quotients [theorem]
  Let (G,u) be a simple dimension group, U a set of traces and Z=Z(ker U) the normalized traces vanishing on ker U; U is refinable iff Z is. (a) If U is refinable, G/ker U has Riesz interpolation and Z is a simplex. (b) If U is good, G/ker U is unperforated. (c) Good sets are refinable. (d) If U is good, G/ker U is a simple dimension group. (e) If Z is refinable and G/ker U is unperforated, ker U has dense image in Z^⊢, the continuous affine functions on S(G,u) vanishing on Z. (f) Under the hypotheses of (e), Z is good.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: False
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: False

integer-valued-polynomial-binomial-basis — Binomial basis of integer-valued polynomials [theorem]
  Every polynomial p∈Q[x] taking integer values on Z has a unique finite expansion p(x)=Σ_j c_j binom(x,j) with c_j∈Z, where binom(x,j)=x(x−1)⋯(x−j+1)/j!. Consequently p has an integer-valued discrete antiderivative P with P(0)=0 and P(n+1)−P(n)=p(n).
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Integer-valued polynomial on Z [both]: The theorem expands an arbitrary integral (integer-valued) polynomial; the proof determines its coefficients from the integer values p(0),…,p(d).
  <- Binomial coefficient [both]: The basis consists of the binomial polynomials binom(x,j)=x(x−1)⋯(x−j+1)/j!; the proof uses their values binom(k,j) at integers and the Pascal relation binom(x+1,j+1)−binom(x,j+1)=binom(x,j).
  <- Bound on the number of distinct polynomial roots [proof]: Uniqueness and the coefficient recursion use that a polynomial of degree ≤d is determined by its values at d+1 distinct points; the same fact identifies D b_(k+1) with b_k from their values at 0,…,k.

bloch-kato-selmer-group — Bloch–Kato Selmer group of a p-adic Galois representation [definition]
  For a number field K and a G_K-stable ℤ_p-lattice T in a continuous p-adic representation V, Sel(K,T)⊂H¹(K,V/T) is the set of classes whose localization at each place v lies in the image of H¹_f(K_v,V). Here H¹_f is 0 at archimedean v, the unramified classes ker[H¹(K_v,V)→H¹(K_v^ur,V)] at v∤p, and ker[H¹(K_v,V)→H¹(K_v,B_cris⊗V)] at v|p, using continuous cohomology.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Continuous cohomology of a profinite group with topological coefficients [statement]: H¹(K_v,V) and H¹(K_v,B_cris⊗V) are continuous cohomology with p-adic coefficients.
  <- First group cohomology with abelian coefficients [statement]: H¹(K,V/T) is cohomology with discrete torsion coefficients.
  <- Place of a number field [statement]: Local conditions are imposed at every place v.
  <- Finite unramified extension of a nonarchimedean local field [statement]: At v∤p the condition uses the maximal unramified extension K_v^ur.
  <- Fontaine's crystalline period ring [statement]: At v|p the finite condition is defined with B_cris.
  <- Lattice in a vector space over a nonarchimedean local field [statement]: T is a Galois-stable lattice in V.
  <- Tensor product of modules over a commutative ring [statement]: B_cris⊗_(ℚ_p)V and V/T=T⊗ℚ_p/ℤ_p.
  <- Kernel of a module homomorphism [statement]: Local conditions and the Selmer group are kernels.

gliding-hump-subspace-approximation — Block approximation of an infinite-dimensional subspace [theorem]
  LetX have a Schauder basis andM⊂X be an infinite-dimensional closed subspace. For any positive summable error boundsε_n, one can choose unit vectorsv_n∈M and successive finite block vectorsu_n with∥v_n−u_n∥<ε_n; the errors can be made small enough that(v_n) and(u_n) are equivalent basic sequences.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete

  <- Equivalent basic sequences [statement]: UnlikeBessaga–Pełczyński, this selects new vectors in an infinite subspace, not a subsequence of a prescribed weakly null sequence.
  <- Uniform boundedness of Schauder partial-sum projections [proof]: At stepn the kernel of the firstm_(n−1) coordinate projection has finite codimension, so its intersection withM is infinite-dimensional. Choose a unitv_n in that intersection. Its Schauder expansion has a sufficiently small tail beyond somem_n, giving a blocku_n supported in(m_(n−1),m_n]. The block norms stay near1 and their coordinate functionals are uniformly bounded. Smaller summable errors make the small-perturbation criterion apply, proving equivalence. This supplies the passage from arbitrary infinite-dimensional subspaces to approximate blocks without assuming any pre-existing sequence is weakly null.
  <- Small perturbation principle for basic sequences [proof]: At stepn the kernel of the firstm_(n−1) coordinate projection has finite codimension, so its intersection withM is infinite-dimensional.   <- Finite-rank linear operator [proof]: At stepn the kernel of the firstm_(n−1) coordinate projection has finite codimension, so its intersection withM is infinite-dimensional. semisimple-p-adic-bowen-volume-lower-bound — Bowen-volume lower bound for semisimple p-adic conjugation [theorem]
  Let G=G₀×G_p, with G₀ a locally compact Hausdorff group and G_p the Q_p-points of a connected reductive algebraic group. For semisimple a∈G_p put H=∑_(|λ|_p>1)log|λ|_p over the eigenvalues of Ad(a), with multiplicity. There is an identity-neighborhood basis consisting of relatively compact open B such that vol(∩_(j=s)^t a^(−j)Ba^j)≥C_B exp(−H(t−s+1)) for all integers s≤0≤t, with C_B>0 and Haar volume on G.

building-apartment-system — Building with an apartment system [definition]

The chambers are the maximal simplices; 𝒜 is an apartment system of X.

burkholder-davis-gundy-inequality — Burkholder–Davis–Gundy inequalities [theorem]
  For each p>0 there are0<c_p≤C_p<∞ such that every real continuous local martingale M starting at zero satisfies c_p E[M]_T^{p/2}≤E sup_{t≤T}|M_t|ᵖ≤C_p E[M]_T^{p/2}, with extended expectations and stopping times T.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Quadratic covariation of continuous semimartingales [statement]: The retained precise mathematical statement/definition uses these immediate inputs; proof inputs are separately classified.
  <- Optional sampling for bounded continuous martingales [proof]: Write M*=sup|M| and Q=√[M]_T. Stop first when |M| reachesλ. The stopped squared-increment martingale and optional sampling give P(M*>2λ,Q≤δλ)≤Cδ²P(M*>λ). For the reverse estimate stop at [M]=λ², then at either [M]=β²λ² or |M−M_τ|=3δλ. The quadratic-variation isometry bounds the conditional expected added bracket by9δ²λ²; on{Q>βλ,M*≤δλ} it is at least(β²−1)λ². Hence P(Q>βλ,M*≤δλ)≤9δ²/(β²−1)P(Q>λ). These are the two good-lambda inequalities. Integrate their tails against pλ^{p−1} for an arbitrary p>0 and chooseδ small enough to absorb the shifted moment on each left-hand side. First localize both M and its bracket and truncate time so moments are finite; monotone convergence removes localization and allows arbitrary stopping times/extended expectations. The tail integration does not require p≥1; this fills the wider p>0 paragraph beyond Hairer’s displayed even-exponent case.
  <- Quadratic-variation isometry for continuous martingales [proof]: Write M*=sup|M| and Q=√[M]_T. Stop first when |M| reachesλ. burnside-basis-theorem-pro-p-groups — Burnside basis theorem for pro-p groups [theorem]
  Let Π be a topologically finitely generated pro-p group and Φ(Π) its Frattini subgroup, the intersection of its maximal open subgroups. gaussian-cameron-martin-covariance-space — Cameron–Martin space of a Hilbert Gaussian measure [definition]
  For a centered Gaussian measure on a real separable Hilbert space with covariance Q, take an eigenbasis Qe_k=q_ke_k. Its Cameron–Martin space consists of u=∑_ku_ke_k with u_k=0 when q_k=0 and∑_{q_k>0}|u_k|²/q_k<∞; that sum is its squared norm. Equivalently it is Range(Q¹ᐟ²) with the minimum preimage norm.

dirichlet-form-capacity — Capacity relative to a Dirichlet form [definition]
  For a Dirichlet form E on L²(X,m) and a strictly positive reference function h=G₁φ (0<φ≤1), Cap_h(U)=inf{E₁(u,u): u∈D(E), u≥h m-a.e. on U} for open U, extended to arbitrary sets by outer approximation with open sets.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Symmetric Dirichlet form [statement]: E, its domain D(E) in L²(X,m), and E₁=E+(·,·)_{L²} are the data of the Dirichlet form. Chen–Ma–Röckner allow non-symmetric forms, but E₁(u,u) involves only the symmetric part and every Dirichlet-form record in this catalogue (nests, quasi-continuity, quasi-regularity) is the symmetric one.
  <- Resolvent of a closed symmetric form [statement]: The reference function is h=G₁φ, the 1-resolvent of the form applied to some φ∈L²(X,m) with 0<φ≤1 m-a.e.
  <- Borel σ-algebra of a topological space [statement]: X is a (Hausdorff) topological space and m is a measure on its Borel σ-algebra; Cap_h is first defined on open sets, which must be measurable for "u≥h m-a.e. on U", and then by outer approximation with open supersets.
  <- Greatest lower bound [statement]: Cap_h(U) and Cap_h(A) are infima of sets of nonnegative extended reals.

cartan-matrix-root-system — Cartan matrix of a root system [definition]
  For a reduced finite crystallographic root system with an ordered simple system α₁,…,α_r, the Cartan matrix is the r×r integer matrix a_ij=⟨α_i∨,α_j⟩=2(α_i,α_j)/(α_i,α_i). It has a_ii=2 and a_ij≤0 for i≠j, d_i·a_ij is symmetric for d_i=(α_i,α_i)/2, and it determines the root system up to isomorphism. For G₂ it is (2 −3; −1 2) in this ordering; some authors use the transpose.

closed-subgroup-theorem-real-lie-group — Cartan’s closed subgroup theorem [theorem]
  Every closed subgroup H of a real Lie group G, with its subspace topology, carries a unique smooth manifold structure making it a real Lie group embedded in G as a submanifold; its Lie algebra is identified with {X∈Lie(G): exp(tX)∈H for every real t}.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Subgroup [statement]: H is a subgroup of G.
  <- Closure of a subset of a topological space [statement]: The hypothesis is that H is closed in G (closed sets are recorded with the closure concept).
  <- Subspace topology [statement]: H carries the subspace topology.
  <- Exponential map of a real Lie group [both]: Lie(H) is described as {X: exp(tX)∈H for all t}.
  <- Exponential coordinates on a real Lie group [proof]: exp is a local homeomorphism (diffeomorphism) near 0, used to write h_n=exp(X_n) (Lemmas 1.3.13–1.3.14; Prop. 1.2.21).
  <- Lie product formula in a real Lie group [proof]: h is closed under addition because exp(t(X+Y)) is a limit of products of elements of H (Exercise 1.2.13(ii)).
  <- Direct sum of vector spaces [proof]: g=h⊕k for a complementary subspace k (Lemma 1.3.14).
  <- Inverse function theorem in Euclidean space [proof]: (Y,Z)↦exp(Y)exp(Z) from h×k to G is a local homeomorphism near the identity (Lemma 1.3.14).
  <- Heine–Borel theorem in finite-dimensional normed spaces [proof]: Z_n/‖Z_n‖ lies on the compact unit sphere of k, so a subsequence converges (Lemmas 1.3.13–1.3.14).

cauchy-goursat-theorem-disk — Cauchy–Goursat theorem for a disk [theorem]
  If f is holomorphic on an open disk D⊆ℂ, with no continuity assumption on f′, then f has a holomorphic primitive on D. Consequently ∫_γf(z)dz=0 for every closed piecewise C¹ path γ in D. The standard proof first shows that integrals over triangles vanish (Goursat’s lemma).
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: False
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: False
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete

  <- Complex line integral along a piecewise smooth path [statement]: The consequence concerns integrals along closed piecewise C¹ paths.

  Evaluation identifies every abelian pro-ℓ group G with (G∨)∨. Under this duality the maximal divisible subgroup of G∨ corresponds to the maximal quotient of G isomorphic to a product of copies of ℤ_ℓ; its coordinate quotients correspond to continuous characters G→ℤ_ℓ.

hyperbolic-plane-characterization — Characterization of the hyperbolic plane [theorem]
  For a nondegenerate two-dimensional quadratic space V over a field of characteristic different from two, the following are equivalent: V is isotropic; V≅⟨1,−1⟩, the hyperbolic plane; V≅⟨a,−a⟩ for every nonzero a; −d(V) is a square. Hence all isotropic nondegenerate binary spaces are isometric.

local-martingale-jump-process-characterization — Characterization of the jump processes of local martingales [theorem]
  Under the usual conditions, let H be a thin process, i.e. {H≠0} lies in a countable union of stopping-time graphs. Then H=ΔX for a local martingale X iff (∑_{s≤t}H_s²)^{1/2} is locally integrable and E[1_{τ<∞}H_τ|F_{τ−}]=0 a.s. for every predictable stopping time τ. X can be chosen purely discontinuous with X₀=0, and is then unique.

chebotarev-frobenius-density — Chebotarev density of Frobenius conjugacy classes [theorem]
  For a finite Galois extension L/K of number fields, each conjugacy class C⊂Gal(L/K) occurs as the Frobenius class of unramified prime ideals of K with Dirichlet density |C|/|Gal(L/K)|. In particular every finite-quotient conjugacy class occurs at infinitely many primes outside any finite excluded set.

choquet-simplex — Choquet simplex [definition]
  A compact convex set in a locally convex real topological vector space for which each point has a unique maximal representing probability measure in the Choquet order. In the metrizable case this is the unique representing probability measure supported on its extreme boundary.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True

The exact simplex predicate is ∀x:K,∃!μ, Rep(μ,x) AND ∀ν,μ≼ν→ν≼μ. This uses actual convex/concave equality predicates:54/59 and integral:157; compact continuity ensures test integrability. It is a bare unique-maximal-representing-measure definition, not a theorem asserting a given K is a simplex.

chow-group-scheme — Chow group of a scheme [definition]
  For a scheme X of finite type over a field, the Chow group A_k(X) is the group Z_k(X) of k-cycles modulo rational equivalence: the subgroup generated by the cycles div(f), viewed on X, for f a nonzero rational function on an integral closed subscheme W⊂X of dimension k+1. A_*(X) denotes ⊕_k A_k(X).
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True

chow-lemma-schemes — Chow’s lemma for separated schemes of finite type [theorem]
  If S is quasi-compact quasi-separated and X→S is separated of finite type, there is a proper surjective S-morphism X′→X, an isomorphism over a dense open subscheme of X, with X′ quasi-projective over S. Nagata’s refinement controls the open on which it is an isomorphism and realizes X′ as a blow-up.

  <- Riesz representation theorem for Hilbert-space functionals [proof]: Give D(E) its complete E₁ inner product and let J:D(E)→H be inclusion. Riesz gives the bounded adjoint, and T=JJ* is bounded, positive, injective and has dense range. Polar decomposition identifies Range(T¹ᐟ²)=Range(J)=D(E), with the E₁ norm represented by T^{-1/2}. Bounded self-adjoint spectral calculus defines A=T^{-1}−I and gives E(u,v)=⟨A¹ᐟ²u,A¹ᐟ²v⟩ onD(E). The same calculus defines the contractions e^{−tA}; dominated convergence gives strong continuity. Conversely, Hille–Yosida gives the generator of a strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroup. Its Laplace-transform resolvent is self-adjoint, so its negative generator is nonnegative self-adjoint. Spectral resolution defines its closed square-root form and recovers the semigroup.

  <- Étale-local lifting of multiplicative-type subgroups of smooth affine group schemes [proof]: Lift a maximal torus T₀ of G⁰_k to an R-torus T⊂G (Proposition 3.1.6); completeness makes T split.

  <- Weyl group of a finite root system [proof]: Both generic and special Weyl groups are W(Φ) for the common root system.
  <- Existence and geometric conjugacy of maximal tori [proof]: Conjugacy of maximal tori in G⁰_k forces every g∈G_k into G⁰_k.
  <- Local constancy of root systems along a split maximal torus [proof]: The split reductive pairs (G_K,T_K) and (G⁰_k,T_k) have isomorphic root systems, by the observation made in the proof of Proposition 3.1.9.

cochain-complex-abelian-category — Cochain complex in an abelian category [definition]
  In an abelian category, a cochain complex C• consists of objects Cⁿ (n∈Z) and morphisms dⁿ:Cⁿ→C^(n+1) with d^(n+1)∘dⁿ=0. A cochain map C•→D• is a family of morphisms commuting with the differentials. The cohomology objects Hⁿ(C•)=ker dⁿ/im d^(n−1) are functorial in cochain maps, and C• is exact exactly when all Hⁿ vanish. Chain complexes are the same objects with decreasing indices, C_n=C^(−n).
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Integer [statement]: Complexes are indexed by integers.
  <- Exact sequence in an abelian category [statement]: A complex is exact when it is an exact sequence, equivalently when its cohomology vanishes.
  Related: Cochain complex of modules — The module-category record over a commutative ring is the special case of complexes in an abelian category.

The critical endpoint is where the two inflections coalesce: substitution gives m_c,J_c,h_c and F″=F‴=0,F⁽⁴⁾<0. Away from it, a degenerate stationary point is a spinodal inflection, not a global maximum, so the retained global maximizers are nondegenerate. The underlying paper has apparent reversed sign typos in the prose of Proposition4’s proof; the displayed derivative(33) and this calculation fix the direction.
  <- Taylor’s theorem with Lagrange remainder [proof]: Write F(m)=−Jm²+p₀((2m−1)J+h) and g=p₀′. Then F′=2J(g−m), F″=−2J+(2J)²g′. The explicit monotone inverse g⁻¹(u)=logu−½log(1−u) reduces the sign of g′−1/(2J) to a quadratic inequality, giving the exact J_c and two inflection branches for J>J_c. Hence there are at most two local maxima; stationary branches vary smoothly when F″≠0 by the implicit-function theorem. stationary-uniform-positive-matrix-product-growth — Common growth exponent for a stationary uniformly positive matrix product [theorem]
  Let (Ω,θ,Q) be an ergodic probability-preserving compact metric system with θ a homeomorphism. Let A:Ω→M_d(ℝ) be continuous and nonnegative, with one fixed-length product A^(s)(ω)=A(θ^(s−1)ω)⋯A(ω) strictly positive for every ω. There is a finite deterministic r such that n⁻¹log‖A^(n)(ω)‖→r and n⁻¹log‖A^(n)(ω)z‖→r for Q-almost every ω and every nonzero z∈ℝ_+ᵈ.

leibman-compact-elements-subgroup — Compact elements at a vector in a nilpotent unitary action [theorem]
  If a nilpotent group G acts unitarily on H and u∈H, then G_c(u)={T∈G:{T^n u:n∈Z} is relatively norm compact} is a subgroup of G.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Nilpotent group [both]: The acting group is assumed nilpotent; the proof replaces G by the subgroup generated by two compact elements, which is nilpotent because γ_i of a subgroup lies in γ_i(G) (Lemma 1.2).
  <- Unitary representation of a topological group [statement]: The hypothesis is a unitary action of the (discrete) group G on a Hilbert space H.
  <- Relatively compact subset of a topological space [both]: G_c(u) consists of T whose orbit {Tⁿu} is precompact, i.e. relatively compact in the norm topology; the proof transfers precompactness between u and its components.
  <- Finitely generated group [proof]: The proof reduces to the finitely generated subgroup ⟨P,Q⟩ generated by two elements compact on u, to which the structure theory applies.
  <- Leibman’s primitive decomposition of a nilpotent unitary action [proof]: Imported Theorem 3.1: H decomposes into G-invariant closed subspaces on each of which the action of ⟨P,Q⟩ is primitive; Corollary 3.2 then works summand by summand.
  <- Orthogonal projection onto a closed Hilbert subspace [proof]: u is split into its projections u_γ onto the invariant summands (and, inside a primitive summand, u_β onto L_β); T is compact on u exactly when compact on every projection, using that T preserves the summands.
  <- Weakly mixing vector of a unitary operator [proof]: Lemmas 2.7 and 2.14: an element of the stabilizer H_β outside E_β is weakly mixing on L_β, and weak mixing excludes a precompact orbit by Lemma 1.15. Leibman’s §1.14 omits the absolute value in the printed Cesàro condition; the intended standard notion (introduction, Theorem 1.16) is used.
  <- Isolator of a subgroup of a nilpotent group [proof]: Proposition 2.10 uses imported Lemma 1.7: the closure (isolator) of the stabilizer H_α is a subgroup in which H_α has finite index, so the classes β are finite and elements outside H_β have no finite cycles on indices.
  <- The normalizer of an isolated nilpotent subgroup is isolated [proof]: Proposition 2.10(3) uses imported Lemma 1.10: the normalizer of the closed (isolated) subgroup Ē_α is closed, giving H_β⊆N(E_α).
  <- Group action on a set [proof]: The primitive structure is an action of G on the index set B of the subspaces L_β, with stabilizers H_β; Lemma 2.14 uses the orbits Tⁿβ.
  <- Compactness of complete totally bounded metric spaces [proof]: Leibman argues with finite ε-nets (Lemma 1.15, componentwise reassembly in Corollary 3.2); precompactness in the complete space H is equivalent to total boundedness.

compactly-supported-l-adic-cohomology — Compactly supported ℓ-adic cohomology [construction]
  Let X be a separated scheme of finite type over a separably closed field k and ℓ a prime different from char k. Then H^i_c(X,Q_ℓ)=(lim_n H^i_c(X,Z/ℓⁿZ))⊗_(Z_ℓ)Q_ℓ. If X is proper, H^i_c(X,Q_ℓ)=H^i(X,Q_ℓ).

  <- Totally bounded metric space [proof]: At each fixed radius, the degree bound and finite mark alphabet permit only finitely many rooted ball types. Successive subsequence extraction and a diagonal subsequence make each ball type eventually constant. Choose compatible representatives inductively and take their increasing union to obtain the rooted limit, retaining full degree/port marks when present. The distance2^{−R}, whereR is the largest agreeing radius, with distance1 if the radius-zero marks disagree and distance0 for agreement at all radii, metrizes local convergence. A Cauchy sequence has stabilizing balls at every radius, so the same union proves completeness. Finitely many ball types give finite covers at each radius, hence total boundedness and compactness; their representatives also give separability. This applies to the paper’s factor templates because all type, weight and port alphabets are finite.

adjacent-center-building-retraction-comparison — Comparison of adjacent-center apartment retractions [theorem]
  Let adjacent C,C′ lie in an apartment A, let H,H′ be the half-apartments containing them and r their common-wall reflection.   <- Gate property for panels in a building [proof]: Garrett’s previous proposition (§15.4 Proposition 1) is the panel trichotomy: when distances differ the nearer chamber lies on a minimal gallery from the farther one; when equal a third chamber C₁ on the panel starts minimal galleries from both, giving δ(C,D)=δ(C′,D).

parabolic-comparison-principle-periodic — Comparison principle for scalar periodic parabolic equations [theorem]
  Let F₁≤F₂ be continuous real functions on [0,T]×S¹×ℝ, one of them locally Lipschitz in u uniformly in (t,x). Let u,v be essentially bounded functions in L²(0,T;H¹(S¹))∩C([0,T];L²(S¹)) with weak time derivatives in L²(0,T;H¹(S¹)*) for the Gelfand triple H¹(S¹)⊂L²(S¹)⊂H¹(S¹)*, solving u_t=u_xx+F₁(t,x,u) and v_t=v_xx+F₂(t,x,v) weakly against H¹(S¹) test functions for almost every t. If u(0)≤v(0) almost everywhere, then u(t)≤v(t) almost everywhere for every t∈[0,T]. Bounded classical solutions are a special case.

  For C*-algebras A,B let Aop,Bop have reversed multiplication and the same star and norm. If φ:A→B is completely positive, then the same linear map φop:Aop→Bop is completely positive; contractivity is also preserved.

monotone-jump-continuous-decomposition — Continuous and jump decomposition of a bounded monotone function [theorem]
  A bounded nondecreasing real function is the sum of a continuous nondecreasing function and an absolutely summable positive linear combination of unit step jumps, allowing each step an intermediate value at its jump point. It has only countably many discontinuities.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Monotone real function [statement]: The defining data or statement explicitly presuppose monotone-function-real.
  <- Sum of a nonnegative series [statement]: The defining data or statement explicitly presuppose nonnegative-series.
  <- Uniform convergence of functions into a metric space [statement]: The defining data or statement explicitly presuppose uniform-convergence.
  <- Continuous map between topological spaces [statement]: One summand is a continuous nondecreasing function, and discontinuities of F are counted.
  <- Countable set [statement]: The statement asserts that F has only countably many discontinuities, and the jump series is indexed by a countable set.
  <- Density of the rationals in the reals [proof]: Each discontinuity x is assigned a rational strictly between F_−(x) and F_+(x).
  <- Countability of the rational numbers [proof]: Distinct discontinuities receive distinct rationals, so the discontinuity set injects into ℚ.
  <- Lebesgue measure on Euclidean space [proof]: The jumps c_x are lengths of disjoint intervals in a bounded interval, so ∑c_x<∞ and the monotonicity of F_c follow by countable additivity of Lebesgue measure.
  <- Continuity of a uniform limit [proof]: The jump series is a uniform limit of finite jump sums, so its discontinuities are exactly the jump points and F−F_pp is continuous.

  <- Positive-power criterion for finite Markov chains [proof]: Take k with Pᵏ strictly positive. Perron–Frobenius gives a unique positive left eigenvectorπ of Pᵏ at eigenvalue1, normalized to sum1. Commutation and normalization implyπP=π. For a positive stochastic matrix, equality in the triangle bound for an eigenvector with|λ|=1 forces all coordinates to have the same complex phase and equal modulus, henceλ=1 and the vector constant. Thus all other eigenvalues ofPᵏ have modulus<1. Jordan normal form makes its nontrivial blocks tend to0, soP^{kn}→1π. Multiplying by finitely many remaining powers provesPⁿ→1π and the finite-state total variation conclusion.
  <- Perron–Frobenius theorem for nonnegative matrices [proof]: Take k with Pᵏ strictly positive. Perron–Frobenius gives a unique positive left eigenvectorπ of Pᵏ at eigenvalue1, normalized to sum1. Commutation and normalization implyπP=π. For a positive stochastic matrix, equality in the triangle bound for an eigenvector with|λ|=1 forces all coordinates to have the same complex phase and equal modulus, henceλ=1 and the vector constant. Thus all other eigenvalues ofPᵏ have modulus<1. Jordan normal form makes its nontrivial blocks tend to0, soP^{kn}→1π. Multiplying by finitely many remaining powers provesPⁿ→1π and the finite-state total variation conclusion.

moment-smoothness-dyadic-convolution-estimate — Convolution estimate trading vanishing moments for smoothness at dyadic scales [theorem]
  Write η_{ν,m}(x)=2^{νn}(1+2^ν|x|)^{−m}. Let k≥0, m₀>n and m₁>n+k. If g has k-th derivatives with |D^γg|≤2^{νk}η_{ν,m₀} for |γ|=k, and h satisfies |h|≤η_{μ,m₁} and has vanishing moments of all orders below k, then |g*h|≤C2^{k(ν−μ)}η_{ν,m₀}*η_{μ,m₁−k}, with C independent of ν,μ. It gives the scale-decay of φ_j*m_Q for dyadic kernels φ_j and smooth molecules m_Q.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: False
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: False
  Prerequisite frontier: elementary ingredients not expanded here.

krasner-eisenstein-distance-formulas — Coordinate and root-product formulas for Eisenstein distance [theorem]
  For monic degree-n Eisenstein f,g over K, d(f,g)=|π|^w with w=min_(0≤i<n)(v_K(g_i−f_i)+i/n). If α=α₁,…,α_n are the roots of f and β is a root of g closest to α, then d(f,g)=∏_(i=1)^n max(|β−α|,|α−α_i|). In particular d is an ultrametric.

coxeter-system — Coxeter system [definition]
  A Coxeter system (W,S) is a group generated by involutions S with only relations (st)^(m_st)=1, where m_ss=1 and m_st=m_ts∈{2,3,…,∞} for s≠t, with∞ imposing no relation. Equivalently any assignment of S to involutions in another group satisfying these relations extends uniquely to a homomorphism from W.

doob-cadlag-martingale-regularization — Càdlàg regularization of a closed martingale [theorem]
  On a usual filtration over a finite horizon, the martingale t↦E[V|F_t] for an integrable terminal variable V has a càdlàg version. This version is uniformly integrable and satisfies E[V|F_tau] at every bounded stopping time tau.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Usual conditions for a filtration [statement]: The filtration is usual.
  <- Continuous-time martingale [statement]: The conditional expectations form a martingale.
  <- Càdlàg path [statement]: The version has càdlàg paths.
  <- Modification (version) of a stochastic process [statement]: “Version” means a modification: equal almost surely at each time.
  <- Uniformly integrable family of real random variables [statement]: The version is uniformly integrable.
  <- σ-algebra of a stopping time [statement]: The identity is conditioned on F_τ.
  <- Càdlàg modification of a submartingale under the usual conditions [proof]: The martingale M_t=E[V|F_t] has constant mean, so under the usual conditions it has a càdlàg modification.
  <- Uniform integrability of the conditional expectations of an integrable variable [proof]: Each M_t is a.s. equal to E[V|F_t], so {M_t} is uniformly integrable.
  <- Optional sampling for a uniformly integrable càdlàg martingale [proof]: For a stopping time τ≤T, optional sampling for the UI càdlàg version gives M_τ=E[M_T|F_τ].
  <- Tower property of conditional expectation [proof]: M_T=E[V|F_T] and F_τ⊆F_T, so E[M_T|F_τ]=E[V|F_τ].

cadlag-semimartingale — Càdlàg semimartingale [definition]
  A real adapted càdlàg process X is a semimartingale if it can locally be written as X=X₀+M+A, where M is a local martingale starting at0 and A is an adapted càdlàg process of locally finite variation starting at0.
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Mathlib formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  Tau Ceti formalization: unknown; LOC unknown/incomplete
  <- Local martingale [statement]: The martingale part is local.
  <- Function of bounded variation on an interval [statement]: The remaining part has locally finite variation.
  <- Adapted stochastic process [statement]: The finite-variation part is adapted.

cepa-multivalued-skorohod-wellposedness — Cépa’s well-posedness theorem for multivalued Skorohod equations [theorem]
  Let η be proper lower semicontinuous convex onℝᵈ with int(dom∂η) nonempty and b globally Lipschitz. For every x∈closure(dom∂η) and continuous w with w₀=0, X=x+w+∫₀^.b(X_s)ds−K has a unique solution in the multivalued Skorohod sense. The map(x,w)↦X is continuous for uniform convergence on compact time intervals. Brownian inputs therefore define a continuous random dynamical system on closure(dom∂η).
  Immediate statement prerequisites complete: True
  Immediate prerequisites for the proof complete: True

  <- Moreau–Yosida envelope and proximal map of a convex function [proof]: Approximate the subdifferential by the Lipschitz gradients of its Moreau–Yosida envelopes and solve the resulting equations after subtracting the fixed continuous driver, using ordinary Picard–Lindelöf. An interior ball in dom∂η gives the coercive graph estimate⟨a(x),x−x₀⟩≥r|a(x)|−C(1+|x|). Subdivide time so the driver oscillation is smaller thanr; in the integration-by-parts estimate the driver–correction term is absorbed into the left-hand variation bound. This yields local uniform state/variation bounds depending on the driver modulus, not its total variation. Parametrize by elapsed time plus accumulated correction variation; the corrections then are uniformly Lipschitz. Helly and Arzelà–Ascoli give a convergent subsequence. The graph inequality identifies the limit: on a flat physical-clock interval the driver and drift integral are constant, so y_r−y_s=−(K_r−K_s). Extend the graph inequality in its fixed state argument to closure(dom∂η) and choose y_s. The continuous bounded-variation quadratic identity gives ∫⟨y_r−y_s,dK_r⟩=−|K_t−K_s|²/2≥0, hence K and y are constant on every such subinterval. The monotone-clock uniform-convergence criterion now permits undoing the clock. Its elementary proof bounds inverse clocks on a compact interval, extracts s_n with τ_n(s_n)=t_n, and uses τ(s)=t and constancy on its level interval; sequential compactness makes convergence uniform. Pass the variational inequalities using the bounded-variation integral limit. For two solutions with the same driver, testing the two graph inequalities against resolvent-regularized averages gives∫⟨X−Y,dK−dL⟩≥0; Grönwall yields uniqueness and continuity in the initial state. The same bounds applied to converging drivers give continuous dependence. Since the construction is pathwise for all continuous inputs and the drift is autonomous, uniqueness gives the flow and shift-cocycle laws without an input-dependent exceptional set. The earlier1995 primary scan supplies the resolvent, monotonicity and time-change identification mechanism; the full1998 printed proof was not accessible, so this deterministic route is explicitly curator-written.
